categories.claim: No: a machine only carries out what its maker or operator has put into it.
categories.reason: The machine executes conceptions supplied from outside (formulae on cards, orders given); interpretation and anticipation of new truths lie with the human who prepares its work.

categories.claim: No: a machine's outputs are fixed by its given data and construction, so nothing in them goes beyond what was put in.
categories.reason: Calculation is determinate: given the data, the results follow necessarily and depend on nothing else.

categories.claim: No: a machine cannot meet new situations or produce fitting new responses, because it acts from the arrangement of its parts, not from reason or will.
categories.reason: Each organ needs a particular arrangement for each action, while reason is a universal instrument; a machine shows no will or mind, only effects that resemble thought.

categories.claim: No: machines are extensions of human faculties and depend on human tending and direction.
categories.reason: Machines obey human consciousness, need human skill to build and feed them, and deliver reports that only humans decipher.

categories.claim: Nothing can originate an idea from nothing, human minds included; new ideas are recombinations of what was received, so the test cannot separate machine from maker.
categories.reason: The understanding can only compound and divide simple ideas it has taken in; invention is adaptation of existing contrivances; imagined monsters are assemblages of stored ideas; one cannot form the idea of an unknown object.

categories.claim: Possibly yes: machines may evolve into a new kind of life or mind that is not supplied by their makers.
categories.reason: New phases of life and consciousness have arisen before, and perfected machines may come to supply, repair and reproduce themselves.

categories.claim: New forms can arise from a mechanism that the conscious agent did not supply, since unconscious bodily processes construct new patterns.
categories.reason: Patterns appear beyond our will and knowledge, constructed by unconscious action of the brain rather than reproduced from earlier impressions.

categories.claim: What an invention produces exceeds what its maker put into it.
categories.reason: The new ideas and feelings an invention releases are out of all proportion to the invention, so the cause releases rather than produces its effect.

categories.claim: Yes: self-repair marks the organism as more than a machine, because it shows a formative power that machines lack.
categories.reason: A machine's parts move one another but do not produce one another, so a watch cannot replace lost parts or mend itself; an organism organizes its materials and restores what it lacks, which mere moving power cannot explain.

categories.claim: Yes: an organism is not a machine, because it continually maintains, renews and rebuilds its own structure.
categories.reason: Living structure is active structure that breaks down and reproduces itself at every moment, so death is not mechanical wearing out; the organism keeps its type while its materials change.

categories.claim: Yes: the organism's capacity to regenerate a whole from divided parts cannot belong to any machine.
categories.reason: A complex machine divided many times cannot remain the whole, yet developing and regenerating organisms do, so no machine can underlie development.

categories.claim: Repair belongs with growth and generation as one organizing process peculiar to living things, which no known physics or chemistry yet explains.
categories.reason: Regeneration and healing are the same synthetic act that forms the organism in the egg; the production of specific form by a whole organism or a piece of it is beyond known physical principles.

categories.claim: No: regeneration and the influence of the whole on the parts are physicochemical processes and do not set the organism apart from mechanism.
categories.reason: Self-reproduction comes from nucleins that catalyse their own synthesis, and regrowth of pieces follows the flow of substances in the sap; no directing force is needed, and nothing shows science cannot reproduce it.

categories.claim: No: the differences vitalists stress, including regeneration and indivisibility, rest on a wrong conception and do not divide organisms from machines.
categories.reason: Divisibility by regeneration is only a matter of degree, organisms are in principle divisible into elementary organisms, and machines show the same mutual conditioning of whole and parts.

categories.claim: No: the body is a machine, more finely made, and like a machine it breaks down and needs outside upkeep.
categories.reason: The body is an automaton made by God with far more parts than human machines; organs wear, fail and need watching and repair, and a broken organism, like a broken clock, does not go on working.

categories.claim: Not necessarily: machines might come to supply, repair and reproduce themselves, so self-repair need not stay a mark of the living.
categories.reason: Machines already reproduce through other agents as clover does through bees, and as they need less tending they may evolve self-repair and reproduction.

categories.claim: Machine wear has a part that cannot be repaired, and machine repair is work done on the machine from outside.
categories.reason: A machine under repair is the object of labour rather than its instrument, and some wear, like that which no doctor can cure, leads to its death.

categories.claim: Machine and detail work diminish the worker's judgment and general intelligence.
categories.reason: Confined to a few simple, unvarying operations, the worker has no occasion to use understanding or invention, loses the habit, and his mind narrows to one detail.

categories.claim: Machinery transfers skill and intellect from the worker into the machine and to those who own or direct it.
categories.reason: Science and the intellectual powers of production are embodied in the mechanism and the master, so the operative's own skill becomes insignificant and the master's mind grows as the worker's shrinks.

categories.claim: Machinery reduces the skill needed to operate it, so less skilled workers and children can do the work.
categories.reason: The machine supplies what hand skill used to supply, turning skilled artisans into overlookers; this opens work to the unskilled and increases competition among workers.

categories.claim: Machinery raises the demand for skill among those who build, repair, improve and superintend it.
categories.reason: Each new machine needs human skill to construct it, devices to feed it, and keener faculties to read and regulate it.

categories.claim: Tending self-acting machines frees the worker's faculties and broadens his outlook compared with old handicraft division of labour.
categories.reason: The machine removes the strain of unremitting dexterity, leaves leisure for thought, is quickly learned, and moving between machines lets the worker consider the whole combination of labour.

categories.claim: Working closely with a machine can develop practical understanding that leads to improving it, but modern machinery has removed that opportunity.
categories.reason: Knowledge of a machine in its running, gained by standing by it, let workers such as the valve boy invent improvements; modern machines need scientific education the workers are refused.

categories.claim: Machine tending demands intense, unrelenting attention that exhausts the worker rather than enlarging him.
categories.reason: The operative must follow the machine's movements and keep the same strain of attention for hours, which wears out the nerves while denying freedom of bodily and intellectual activity.

categories.claim: Making the worker into a precise instrument destroys his intellectual and creative capacity.
categories.reason: Demanding tool-like precision from men forces all their spirit into the mean act and unhumanizes them; the machine uses the worker as its appendage and drains work of interest.

categories.claim: Machine work changes the kind of intelligence a worker has rather than simply raising or lowering it.
categories.reason: Habituation to the machine process sharpens thinking suited to that process and weakens older forms of intelligence; the difference is one of kind and direction.

categories.claim: Under scientific management machine workers are trained upward into more skilled and interesting work.
categories.reason: Management develops the science the worker cannot grasp alone and teaches him, so laborers learn machinist's work and machinists move to more intricate machines and teaching.

categories.claim: Repetitive machine work does not harm most workers, who prefer not to think on the job.
categories.reason: Most minds do not find repetition terrifying and want jobs that require no thought; sympathy for them projects the restlessness of creative minds.

categories.claim: Whether the worker's mind is diminished depends on his understanding of and care for the whole process.
categories.reason: If the worker sees the whole process his part serves and cares for it, the mechanizing effect is counteracted; a mere tender has no insight.

categories.claim: Machinery should take over dull, unintellectual labour, leaving people free for other activity.
categories.reason: Monotonous and unpleasant labour belongs to machines; its harms come from private ownership, not from the machine.

categories.claim: Yes: people who rely on writing stop exercising memory, so memory weakens and they gain the appearance of knowledge without the substance.
categories.reason: Memory weakens when it is not used; trusting external marks replaces remembering from within, giving reminders rather than knowledge.

categories.claim: Yes: notebooks and stored information weaken memory, as one case of tools that make the user lose the faculty they replace.
categories.reason: Each convenience (coach, watch, almanac, notebook) removes the need to use a bodily or mental skill, and the unused skill is lost.

categories.claim: Writing partly ruins memory but this is outweighed, because the written record serves as a larger and more faithful memory.
categories.reason: Writing makes memory partly dispensable, yet a tablet lets one recover everything exactly and without effort, taking the place of the most extensive memory.

categories.claim: Memory moves outside the person into written aids, which become part of an extended self rather than a loss.
categories.reason: Tools such as the pocket-book are extra-corporeal limbs that man adds to himself as he develops.

categories.claim: No: writing things down helps memory, because notes and abstracts give handles for recall and secure what would otherwise be lost.
categories.reason: Brief written compends can be reviewed often, writing supplies handles for recollection, and ideas not noted at the moment fade; those who never write need double natural memory.

categories.claim: Copying and marking texts does not help memory and wastes effort; attention and rereading do the work.
categories.reason: Writing distracts the thoughts and the hand has no closer link to memory than the eye; what is read twice is remembered better than what is transcribed.

categories.claim: Written records preserve facts more precisely and stably than memory and oral tradition, which change and decay.
categories.reason: Oral transmission alters words and facts as they pass mouth to ear; writing fixes them in a form less liable to change.

categories.claim: Societies without reliance on writing achieved feats of memory that writing-dependent people find nearly impossible.
categories.reason: Vedic texts were preserved entirely by oral learning, so exactly that reciters can correct a printed edition; easier contrivances replaced greater individual effort.

categories.claim: Before writing was common, communities used verse and bodily devices to hold laws in memory.
categories.reason: Laws were put into verse so people could retain them by singing and reciting.

categories.claim: Invention carries out a divine purpose by restoring the dominion over nature that God gave to mankind.
categories.reason: Power over nature is a right assigned by God's gift, and searching out what God concealed is a king's glory; abuse is no objection, since every worldly good can be abused.

categories.claim: Invention continues or imitates God's own creative work.
categories.reason: Inventions are new creations in imitation of divine works; machines are a new kind of being called into existence through man, which shows his creative and royal calling.

categories.claim: Technical works fulfil God's plan to join the earth and its peoples together.
categories.reason: Spanning the earth with networks, crossing oceans and welding lands together was God's purpose from the first, so engineers and inventors serve it and will be justified when its spiritual meaning is revealed.

categories.claim: Great organized works of improvement are the means by which religion (Christianity) should now achieve its aim.
categories.reason: The religious aim is the improvement of the poorest class, and a general plan of works to make the earth productive best serves it and makes Christianity prevail.

categories.claim: Human technical progress is the continuous carrying out of one vast design.
categories.reason: Unlike animals, mankind has added generation after generation to a single edifice whose progress has never ceased, always in fulfilment of one design.

categories.claim: The Creator's goodness implies that inventions must benefit mankind, not destroy labour.
categories.reason: If the mind's discoveries reduced labour and welfare, the Creator would have given man faculties that destroy each other, which is unthinkable; the facts also show more labour where there are more inventions.

categories.claim: Invention serves a divine purpose only when directed by religion or love; directed by gain it does not.
categories.reason: The cruel aspect of mills and railways comes from the mercenary ends they obey; wielded by love, science and its works become continuations of creation. Power over nature should be governed by right reason and true religion.

categories.claim: Invention serves an end beyond what the inventor intends, raising humanity above itself, without this being called divine.
categories.reason: The consequences of an invention are out of proportion to it: its new ideas and feelings enlarge our horizon, as though the grip of intelligence on matter mainly releases something matter holds back.

categories.claim: Technology has no bearing on divine truth.
categories.reason: Divine truth is fixed in scripture and cannot progress; no invention from the compass to vaccination affects any theological question.

categories.claim: Faith in technology has displaced faith in the divine and become a false religion.
categories.reason: Men have lost belief in the Invisible and made Mechanism their deity; rationalism made technics a materialist religion with its own Trinity; the railway to the Celestial City lets pilgrims keep their sins and skip the Cross.

categories.claim: Invention is a usurpation of God's place rather than the fulfilment of his purpose.
categories.reason: The inventor's dream is to build a world and be God, so the machine has been felt as devilish; every great invention has been hailed as an insult to some god; man has nearly become a god himself by artificial means, though not happily.

categories.claim: Technology repeats the Fall: the creature revolts against its creator and threatens man's divine image.
categories.reason: Machines dictate their own laws, replace men and turn them into machines; man is the image of God and cannot become the image of the machine without ceasing to exist.

categories.claim: Invention springs from the inventor's personal drive, not from any purpose about its consequences.
categories.reason: The inventor's passion has nothing to do with its consequences; it is his personal life-drive.

categories.claim: Transcendent, supernatural aspirations are what drive the building of material civilization.
categories.reason: Even the irreligious imagine a superhuman event perfecting the world, and these aspirations, remote from the physical world, built material civilization.

categories.claim: Delight or attachment toward a made thing does not survive the discovery that it is made.
categories.reason: The feeling rested on the thought that nature produced the object; once it is known as imitation that thought is gone, and the interest disappears or turns to vanity.

categories.claim: Love for an artificial being can stay genuine when its nature is known, because what is loved is the form or likeness it bears, not its material.
categories.reason: The lover loves the figure the thing presents or its resemblance to a beloved, whatever body carries it or whoever made it.

categories.claim: Love for a known artificial being is no less genuine than love for a woman, since all such love is already an illusion.
categories.reason: Passion cannot get outside a personal illusion and women themselves are partly artificial, so replacing one illusion with another loses nothing.

categories.claim: Love for an artificial being lasts only while its artificial nature is unacknowledged.
categories.reason: The lover refuses to own that the thing is ivory or a doll, or is held by a spell; breaking the deception would show it as a hollow image.

categories.claim: Love for an artificial being can be fulfilled only if the being becomes, or shows itself to be, living and thinking.
categories.reason: Pygmalion asks for a wife like the statue and loves her once she warms; lovers demand signs that a mistress thinks and feels before trusting their love.

categories.claim: Once the thing is seen for what it is, the love given to it turns out to have been meant for something else, and turns to estrangement or hatred.
categories.reason: The doll returns nothing; the tenderness poured into it was aimed at an invisible soul for which the doll was only a pretext.

categories.claim: Love for an automaton is not love for another but a narcissistic attachment that estranges the lover from real objects.
categories.reason: The doll is a detached part of the lover's own psyche confronting him as a person, so the love is compulsive and self-directed.

categories.claim: Discovering that the beloved is a mechanism breaks the lover rather than the love surviving.
categories.reason: Seeing the doll's eyes torn out and the automaton carried off drives the lover into madness.

categories.claim: Artificial beings can genuinely love one another.
categories.reason: Made beings cut off from others attach more closely to each other, or refuse to live without each other and say they belong to each other.

categories.claim: Love between artificial beings may fail because each may loathe the made form in the other.
categories.reason: A creature that hates its own deformity may hate it more in its mate, and the mate may prefer human beauty.

categories.claim: A being made artificial cannot love, so love toward it cannot be returned.
categories.reason: A tin body contains no heart, and without a heart no one can love.
